ad19a4b36fa75167.h:
Influence abroad · funding cut / gag rule

Kemp-Kasten amendment and U.S. withholding from UNFPA

1985-present · Washington, D.C. · United States
Line to China, one of the countries it is aimed at.

Congress first enacted the Kemp-Kasten amendment in 1985, after the Reagan administration temporarily withheld some UNFPA funding in 1984 over concerns about China's population policies. It bars U.S. funds to any organization or programme that the president determines supports or participates in the management of a programme of coercive abortion or involuntary sterilization. KFF says it has only ever been applied to UNFPA and has been used to withhold UNFPA funding in 20 of the past 41 fiscal years.

U.S. Congress and President
Aimed at

Influence abroad · funding cut / gag rule

U.S.-funded contraceptives held in Belgian warehouse slated for destruction

2025 · Geel, Belgium · United States
Line to Democratic Republic of the Congo, one of the countries it is aimed at.

U.S.-funded contraceptives sat in a Kuehne+Nagel warehouse in Geel, Belgium, after the Trump administration's freeze on foreign aid, and in July 2025 the State Department said it would incinerate them. According to IPPF, 77% of the stock was earmarked for DR Congo, Kenya, Tanzania, Zambia and Mali. As of September 16, 2025 the stock's fate was unclear after Belgian authorities found it still in the warehouse.

Influence abroad · population-control programme abroad

USAID sponsorship of Peru's family planning programme (1996-2000)

1996-2000 · Lima · United States
Line to Peru, one of the countries it is aimed at.

From 1996 to 2000 Peru's government ran an aggressive National Program of Reproductive Health and Family Planning; a Peruvian Congress report (2002) using health-ministry data counted around 311,000 tubal ligations and 25,000 vasectomies. The congressional commission concluded the sterilizations were essentially non-voluntary. Economist Silvio Rendon estimates 211,000 women were sterilized without being fully informed (1993-2000) and states that USAID 'was a sponsor of this program'; no USAID dollar figure is given.

c8e9ec5ff9bf379e.h:
Coercion · forced or coerced sterilization

Peru's sterilization campaign under Fujimori (PNSRPF)

1996–2000 · Lima · Peru

The health ministry ran sterilization quotas under the National Reproductive Health and Family Planning Programme. Women were operated on without free and informed consent, sometimes without adequate medical care. Some women died after the operations, including Mamérita Mestanza and Celia Ramos (died 1997).

Targeted
Mainly poor, rural, Indigenous (Quechua and Aymara) women; also men
Scale
Figures differ by source. Wikipedia 'Forced sterilization in Peru': official count of 260,874 sterilizations and 21,494 vasectomies under the programme, 1996–2000; several sources estimate over 300,000. Global Voices (citing the Prosecutor's Office report): 'More than 272,000 women and 22,000 men'. Inter-American Court, Ramos Durand v. Peru (para. 52, via Opinio Juris): about 314,605 women and 24,563 men subjected to the PNSRPF, 1996–2000. Wikipedia 'Compulsory sterilization' cites a July 2002 final report: 331,600 women and 25,590 men, 1995–2000. Giulia Tamayo (Flora Tristán) found only 10% of 314,967 women gave free, prior and informed consent. The victims' registry (REVIESFO) lists 'more than 8,000' people. Health workers received US$4–10 per woman. Wikipedia 'Alberto Fujimori': 'over 215,000 people, mostly women, entirely indigenous, were forced or threatened into sterilization' and 16,547 men had vasectomies, against 80,385 sterilizations and 2,795 vasectomies in the three years before. The same article says a 2002 report by Health Minister Fernando Carbone suggested Fujimori was involved in the forced sterilization of up to 300,000 Indigenous women, 1996–2000.
Accountability
IACHR received the Mamérita Mestanza case in 1999. Peruvian prosecutors filed and shelved the case repeatedly (Global Voices: eight times over two decades); in December 2021 Judge Rafael Martínez opened proceedings against Fujimori and former health ministers; in December 2023 the Supreme Court annulled that process and sent the case back to the prosecutor's office. CEDAW (October 2024) said the policy 'could constitute a crime against humanity'. In 2024 a Chilean justice approved adding forced-sterilization charges to Fujimori's extradition framework (Wikipedia). On 5 March 2026 the Inter-American Court ruled Peru responsible in Ramos Durand et al. v. Peru (Celia Ramos, died 1997), ordering investigations, a reparations policy for all victims, and about US$340,000 for her family (as reported).
Sources
  1. Forced sterilization in Peru (Wikipedia)
  2. Alberto Fujimori (Wikipedia)
  3. Peru's Supreme Court annuls the judicial process for forced sterilizations (Global Voices)
  4. Forced sterilisation and transformative reparations: Ramos Durand et al. v. Peru (Opinio Juris, 18 Aug 2026)
  5. Inter-American Court finds Peru guilty of forced sterilization (Center for Reproductive Rights, 6 Mar 2026)
  6. Compulsory sterilization (Wikipedia)

Nazi Germany's Law for the Prevention of Hereditarily Diseased Offspring

1934–1945 · Berlin · Germany

Enacted 14 July 1933 and in force from January 1934, the law set up Genetic Health Courts of a judge and two doctors that ordered sterilizations. It applied to the general population, not only to people in institutions. Of nearly 4,000 appeals in 1934, 3,559 failed.

Targeted
People with conditions listed in the law (e.g. 'congenital mental deficiency', schizophrenia, hereditary blindness or deafness, severe alcoholism) — many not actually hereditary
Scale
1934: 84,600 cases brought to the courts, 62,400 forced sterilizations; 1935: 88,100 trials and 71,700 sterilizations (Edwin Black citing Henry Friedlander). Over 400,000 people sterilized against their will by the end of the regime (Wikipedia).
Accountability
The Wikipedia article checked does not cover postwar accountability or compensation (not verified).

Lebensborn

1935–1945 · Steinhöring, near Munich · Germany

Heinrich Himmler founded Lebensborn on 12 December 1935 to raise births to parents the SS judged racially desirable. It ran maternity homes in Germany and occupied Norway and handled children taken from occupied countries for adoption by German families.

Births to SS-approved 'racially valuable' parents; children taken from occupied countries
Scale
About 8,000 children born in Lebensborn homes in Germany and a similar number in Norway. Kidnapping estimates: Polish government 10,000 (under 15% returned); other estimates up to 200,000; historian A. Dirk Moses thinks about 20,000 more likely (all per Wikipedia).
Accountability
Nuremberg RuSHA trial: of about 10,000 foreign-born children found in the US zone, 340 had been handled by Lebensborn; the accused were acquitted on kidnapping charges. Forced abortions and infant deaths among Polish and Soviet forced labourers

1943–1945 · Velpke, Lower Saxony · Germany

A decree of 11 March 1943 allowed abortions 'requested' by Eastern and civilian workers; women who refused were threatened with prison or starvation. Abortions were enforced after checking whether the father was German. Babies who were born were taken from their mothers and many died of neglect in special homes.

Targeted
Pregnant Polish and Soviet ('Ostarbeiter') forced labourers and their babies
Scale
Roughly 100,000 infants of Polish and Soviet forced labourers killed by forced abortion or neglect in 1943–1945; other estimates up to 200,000. About 400 'Ausländerkind-Pflegestätte' homes; average mortality over 50%. Velpke: 76 Polish and 15 Soviet babies starved in 1944 (all per Wikipedia).
Accountability
Velpke trial: a British military court in Brunswick tried Heinrich Gerike and seven others, 20 March–3 April 1946, for killing Polish children by wilful neglect; two death sentences.

Governor Mark Warner apologized in 2002, on the 75th anniversary of Buck v. Bell. In 2015 Virginia began paying $25,000 to each victim alive on 1 February 2015.

Patients in state hospitals and homes, and prisoners

Native American women treated by the Indian Health Service

'La Operación' — mass sterilization in Puerto Rico

Law 116 of 1937 legalized sterilization and set up eugenics boards. Sterilization became the most common form of birth control, encouraged by US and island officials; in 1968 over a third of women did not know tubal ligation was permanent.

Puerto Rican women of childbearing age

Historian Iris López says it was 'largely driven by the Puerto Rican government and the Puerto Rican people themselves' — the degree of coercion is debated.

The sterilization law and eugenics board were repealed in 1960. No apology or compensation found.

The Shah Commission investigated Emergency abuses (the findings checked concern demolitions, not sterilization totals). No compensation found.

078f683d4f9f6b3e.h:
Coercion · forced or coerced sterilization

Bilaspur sterilization camp deaths

2014 · Pendari, Bilaspur district, Chhattisgarh · India

Women were sterilized in mass camps under state targets. Within two days many fell ill; a preliminary report found tablets given to them contained zinc phosphide, a rat poison chemical.

Targeted
Poor women at state-run sterilization camps
Scale
About 140 women operated on in two camps on 8 November 2014; 15 died and 70 were hospitalized (Wikipedia). One surgeon did '83 sterilizations in six hours' against a guideline of 30 per day. India: close to 1,000 deaths a year linked to public-health sterilizations (Down to Earth).
Accountability
Government promised about $6,600 per affected family. On 14 September 2016, in Devika Biswas v. Union of India, the Supreme Court ordered camp-based sterilizations stopped within three years and told governments to avoid targets that push workers into forced sterilization.

Poor women and men

Incentive of 2,000 taka for tubal ligation or vasectomy, 300 taka to the referrer; a 1977 study found 40–60% of men chose vasectomy because of the payment. Ershad's 1982 programme aimed to sterilize 1.4 million people in two years with 40,000 field workers. Deaths: 21.3 per 100,000 sterilizations (1979–80) and 19 deaths among 153,032 sterilizations (1980–81) (Wikipedia).

None found.

Under communist rule and after, doctors sterilized Romani women without their consent. Charter 77 dissidents called it genocide in 1977–78.

Romani women

Government apologized in 2009. A 2021 law grants 300,000 crowns to women illegally sterilized between 1966 and 2012, with three years to apply.

Women across the Soviet Union

HIV-positive women giving birth in public hospitals

027228b838016d6b.h:
Incentive · raise births

Quebec Allowance for Newborn Children

1988–1997 · Quebec City · Canada

Quebec paid families a cash allowance after each birth, with by far the largest amount for third and later children. The programme was cancelled in 1997. Milligan's study compared Quebec with the rest of Canada and found the gap in birth rates nearly closed while it ran. A later Quebec family minister called the bonuses an 'abject failure'.

What was offered or said
Cash per birth that grew with birth order. In 1988: $500 for a first child, $500 for a second, $3,000 for a third or later child (eight quarterly payments of $375). By 1992: $500 first, $1,000 second, $8,000 for a third or later child (20 quarterly payments of $400).
Measured effect
Kevin Milligan, 'Subsidizing the Stork' (NBER WP 8845, 2002; Review of Economics and Statistics 87(3), 2005) found 'a strong effect of the policy on fertility'. As reported by the Globe and Mail, fertility rose 12% overall and 25% for families eligible for the $8,000 payment. Milligan's C.D. Howe backgrounder estimated 93,068 extra births in 1989–96 (14.5% above the no-programme simulation) at roughly $15,000 per extra birth.
Sources
  1. Subsidizing the Stork: New Evidence on Tax Incentives and Fertility (NBER w8845)
  2. Paying the stork worked in Quebec (Globe and Mail)
  3. Milligan backgrounder (C.D. Howe Institute)
Place: Quebec City. Position from GeoNames city point, via github.com/lutangar/cities.json.

b590caf309c5b184.h:
Incentive · raise births

Maternity capital

2007–present · Moscow · Russia

Russia introduced maternity capital in 2007 to encourage second and third children. The money is paid as a restricted voucher rather than cash. Studies disagree on how much it changed births.

What was offered or said
A one-time state voucher for mothers who give birth to or adopt a second or later child from 1 January 2007: 250,000 rubles (about US$10,000) in 2007. It can be spent only on housing, a child's education, or the mother's pension (later also some healthcare).
Measured effect
Slonimczyk and Yurko (2012, HSE working paper) estimated the policy had 'almost no effect in increasing the number of births'. Studies cited by Proshin (2023) found the effect was larger on second births than first births (Slonimczyk and Yurko, 2014) and larger in regions where the payment was big relative to housing prices (Sorvachev and Yakovlev, 2020); official monthly data suggest an effect beginning around August 2007.
Sources
  1. Impact of Child Subsidies on Child Health… (Proshin, European Journal of Population, 2023)
  2. Assessing the Impact of the Maternity Capital Policy in Russia (Slonimczyk & Yurko, 2012)
  3. Baby bonus (Wikipedia)
